concepts.title: Amplitude, frequency and phase
concepts.canDo: Read amplitude, frequency and phase from a sinusoidal signal and convert Hz to rad/s.

misconceptions.statement: Entering 100 in a rad/s field produces 100 Hz.
misconceptions.correction: 100 rad/s is about 15.92 Hz; convert with 2*pi*f.

explanation.keyIdea: A sinusoid is x(t)=A sin(2*pi*f*t+phi): A is amplitude, f is frequency in Hz and phi is phase in radians.
explanation.text: A sinusoidal signal repeats smoothly over time. Amplitude measures its peak size, frequency counts cycles per second, and phase describes its position within a cycle relative to a reference. For x(t)=A sin(2*pi*f*t+phi), time is in seconds, f is in Hz and phi is in radians. The period is T=1/f. A 100 Hz signal therefore repeats every 0.01 s. Some software fields require angular frequency rather than Hz: enter omega=2*pi*f rad/s. Changing amplitude does not itself change frequency. Always read the axis units before comparing waveforms.

visual.description: Draw two labelled time traces with equal frequency and different amplitudes; a third trace has a phase shift. Show 10 ms period for 100 Hz.
visual.alt: Amplitude, frequency and phase; Peak size: amplitude. Cycles per second: frequency. Relative timing: phase. Convert Hz using 2*pi*f.

concepts.title: Message, carrier and the purpose of modulation
concepts.canDo: Distinguish the message from the carrier and describe which carrier property each modulation family changes.

misconceptions.statement: The carrier alone contains the message.
misconceptions.correction: Information is represented by the carrier changes caused by the message.

explanation.keyIdea: Modulation changes a carrier property according to a message; demodulation recovers the message at the receiver.
explanation.text: The message signal contains the information we want to convey. The carrier is a reference oscillation used to place that information into a suitable transmission frequency range. Modulation changes a property of the carrier according to the message. Amplitude modulation changes its amplitude, while angle modulation changes frequency or phase. Demodulation is the corresponding recovery process at the receiver. In our teaching model, the message is a 100 Hz sinusoid and the carrier is 2000 Hz. These are chosen laboratory values, not a claim about radio broadcast frequencies. A carrier alone does not contain the selected message.

visual.alt: Message, carrier and the purpose of modulation; Message is information; carrier is a reference; modulation prepares transmission; demodulation recovers information.

concepts.title: Conventional AM, envelope and modulation index
concepts.canDo: Interpret the conventional AM envelope and calculate modulation index for a single-tone message.

misconceptions.statement: An envelope detector works equally well on DSB-SC.
misconceptions.correction: DSB-SC changes sign with the message; simple envelope detection loses that sign.

explanation.keyIdea: For a single tone, conventional AM is s(t)=Ac[1+mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t)]cos(2*pi*fc*t).
explanation.text: Conventional AM retains a carrier component and varies the surrounding envelope with the message. For a normalised single-tone message, s(t)=Ac[1+mu*cos(2*pi*fm*t)]cos(2*pi*fc*t), where mu is the modulation index. An envelope detector can follow the message when the envelope stays non-negative and its time constant is suitable. With 0<=mu<=1, the envelope does not cross zero; mu>1 causes overmodulation and distorts simple envelope recovery. If the envelope extrema are Emax and Emin, mu=(Emax-Emin)/(Emax+Emin). This envelope rule applies to conventional AM; it must not be applied blindly to DSB-SC.

visual.description: Compare conventional AM envelopes for mu=0.5 and mu=1.5; show zero crossings and label envelope distortion rather than implying all demodulators fail.
visual.alt: Conventional AM, envelope and modulation index; Conventional AM includes carrier plus sidebands. For ordinary envelope recovery, keep mu at or below one.

concepts.title: DSB-SC generation and sidebands
concepts.canDo: Build the DSB-SC product signal and locate the sidebands for a zero-mean single-tone message.

misconceptions.statement: Suppressed carrier means no transmitted signal.
misconceptions.correction: The two sidebands still carry the message; the separate carrier line is suppressed.

explanation.keyIdea: DSB-SC is s(t)=Ac*m(t)*cos(2*pi*fc*t); a zero-mean single-tone message produces sidebands at fc-fm and fc+fm.
explanation.text: DSB-SC is double-sideband suppressed-carrier amplitude modulation. Multiply a zero-mean message by a carrier to produce s(t)=Ac*m(t)*cos(2*pi*fc*t). For a sinusoidal message at fm, the product contains components at fc-fm and fc+fm: the lower and upper sidebands. Unlike conventional AM, no carrier offset is deliberately added. With a zero-mean message, there is no separate spectral carrier line at fc in the ideal model. A message DC offset can reintroduce that line. For fm=100 Hz and fc=2000 Hz, the sidebands are 1900 and 2100 Hz. Suppressed carrier does not mean that the transmitted signal is zero.

visual.description: Plot a single-tone DSB-SC magnitude spectrum at 1900 and 2100 Hz, no separate 2000 Hz line under zero-mean ideal assumptions; accompany with signed time waveform.
visual.alt: DSB-SC generation and sidebands; Product modulation; two sidebands; no intentional carrier offset; simple envelope detection is insufficient.

concepts.title: SSB and VSB compared with DSB-SC
concepts.canDo: Compare DSB-SC, SSB and VSB bandwidth and identify what spectrum each transmits.

explanation.keyIdea: SSB sends one sideband; VSB sends one sideband plus a vestige of the other.
explanation.text: Amplitude-modulation variants differ in which spectral components they transmit. DSB-SC sends both sidebands, requiring bandwidth 2B for a message whose highest frequency is B. SSB sends only one sideband and ideally requires bandwidth B, making better use of a restricted channel. VSB sends one sideband with a small vestige of the other; its bandwidth lies between ideal SSB and full DSB for a comparable message. The vestige eases practical filtering near the carrier. These are spectrum choices, not separate message types. Our lab uses DSB-SC, so SSB and VSB implementation is outside the lab route, although their comparison belongs in this chapter.

visual.alt: SSB and VSB compared with DSB-SC; For message bandwidth B: DSB-SC uses 2B; ideal SSB uses B; VSB retains a vestige.

concepts.title: Coherent demodulation and recovery gain
concepts.canDo: Explain product detection and the gain needed to recover the message under a matched unit-amplitude receiver carrier.

misconceptions.statement: The receiver can use an arbitrary carrier frequency or phase.
misconceptions.correction: Coherent recovery requires carrier alignment; mismatch reduces or changes the message.

explanation.keyIdea: Multiply DSB-SC by a matched local carrier, lowpass-filter it, and use gain 2 to undo the product factor for unit carrier amplitudes.
explanation.text: A coherent receiver multiplies the DSB-SC signal by a local oscillator matched to the transmitted carrier in frequency and phase. For unit-amplitude carriers, the product is m(t)*cos^2(2*pi*fc*t). Using cos^2(theta)=[1+cos(2*theta)]/2, this contains m(t)/2 plus a high-frequency term around twice the carrier. Lowpass filtering removes that high-frequency term while retaining the message band. A recovery gain of 2 restores the ideal message amplitude when both carrier amplitudes are one. A practical filter can still alter amplitude and phase slightly. Coherent recovery preserves message sign, whereas a simple envelope detector cannot recover a general signed DSB-SC message correctly.

concepts.title: Lowpass filtering and waveform comparison
concepts.canDo: Choose a lowpass stage that retains the message and compare outputs with appropriate allowance for filter response.

misconceptions.statement: A real lowpass filter gives an exactly identical output trace.
misconceptions.correction: It can introduce attenuation, phase lag and startup transients.

explanation.keyIdea: A lowpass filter retains lower-frequency components and attenuates higher-frequency components.
explanation.text: A lowpass filter is the separation stage after product detection. Its useful passband must include the message frequencies while its attenuation rejects the components near twice the carrier. Our bounded model uses a 100 Hz message, a 2000 Hz carrier and a second-order Butterworth lowpass with 500 Hz cutoff. In a continuous Transfer Fcn block, H(s)=wc^2/(s^2+sqrt(2)*wc*s+wc^2), where wc=2*pi*500 rad/s. This filter does not remove every unwanted component perfectly. It introduces a startup transient and frequency-dependent phase lag. Compare the recovered signal after startup, checking frequency and amplitude while allowing the predicted phase shift rather than demanding an identical trace.

concepts.title: Carrier mismatch and debugging
concepts.canDo: Predict coherent-receiver phase/frequency error effects and correct the responsible model parameter.

misconceptions.statement: 90 degree mismatch guarantees every sample of a finite-filter output is exactly zero.
misconceptions.correction: The ideal message component vanishes, but finite-filter high-frequency residuals can remain.

explanation.keyIdea: With frequency matched and unit carrier amplitudes, ideal gain-corrected recovery is m(t)*cos(phi), where phi is relative phase error.
explanation.text: Carrier mismatch is a receiver alignment problem, not automatically a failed transmitter. With equal carrier frequencies, a relative phase error phi scales the ideal recovered message by cos(phi) after gain correction. A 60 degree error leaves half amplitude; a 90 degree error suppresses the ideal message-band component. A finite filter can leave residual high-frequency ripple, so the observed trace need not be perfectly zero. A frequency mismatch adds a time-varying factor and can create a beating or distorted recovered waveform. Inspect the transmitter first, then compare the local oscillator frequency and phase with the carrier before changing unrelated blocks.

concepts.title: Frequency modulation and deviation
concepts.canDo: Identify FM behaviour and estimate single-tone bandwidth using Carson’s rule.

misconceptions.statement: FM bandwidth is always twice the message bandwidth.
misconceptions.correction: FM occupied bandwidth also depends on frequency deviation.

explanation.keyIdea: FM varies instantaneous carrier frequency with the message while ideal carrier amplitude remains constant.
explanation.text: Frequency modulation, or FM, represents the message through changes in instantaneous carrier frequency rather than through carrier amplitude. An ideal FM signal has constant amplitude. Frequency deviation Delta f is the maximum departure from the carrier frequency. For a sinusoidal message of frequency fm, the modulation index is beta=Delta f/fm. FM generally has multiple sidebands, so its bandwidth is not simply the DSB-SC value 2B. Carson’s rule estimates a useful occupied bandwidth as approximately 2*(Delta f+B), where B is the highest message frequency. This is an engineering approximation, not an exact finite spectral boundary. FM is part of the chapter but not required to execute our selected DSB-SC lab.

concepts.title: Phase modulation and FM–PM distinction
concepts.canDo: Distinguish PM from FM and explain the link between phase change and instantaneous frequency.

misconceptions.statement: FM and PM have identical direct dependence on the message.
misconceptions.correction: FM frequency follows the message; PM phase follows it.

explanation.keyIdea: PM varies carrier phase directly with the message: s(t)=Ac*cos(2*pi*fc*t+kp*m(t)).
explanation.text: Phase modulation, or PM, changes the instantaneous phase of a constant-amplitude carrier directly according to the message. Its form is s(t)=Ac*cos(2*pi*fc*t+kp*m(t)), where kp is phase sensitivity. FM and PM are both angle modulation, but their direct message relationships differ: FM frequency deviation follows the message, while PM phase deviation follows the message. Because instantaneous frequency is the rate of change of phase divided by 2*pi, PM frequency deviation follows the derivative of the message. A constant message produces a fixed phase shift in PM rather than a sustained frequency offset. PM completes our chapter comparison and is not a prerequisite for the selected lab.

glosses.or: ଦୁଇଟି Sideband ଥାଏ ଏବଂ ଅଲଗା Carrier component ଦମିତ ଥାଏ।

terms.definition: A frequency component or band created around the carrier by modulation.

glosses.or: Modulation ଦ୍ୱାରା Carrier ଚାରିପାଖରେ ଉତ୍ପନ୍ନ Frequency ଅଂଶ।

terms.definition: Absence of an intentionally retained carrier spectral component in the ideal zero-mean model.

glosses.or: ଅଲଗା Carrier spectral component କୁ ରଖାଯାଏ ନାହିଁ।

terms.definition: Single-sideband amplitude modulation.

glosses.or: କେବଳ ଗୋଟିଏ Sideband ପଠାଇବା।

terms.definition: Vestigial-sideband amplitude modulation.

glosses.or: ଗୋଟିଏ Sideband ସହିତ ଅନ୍ୟଟିର ଛୋଟ ଅଂଶ ପଠାଇବା।

terms.definition: The width of a specified frequency range.

glosses.or: Signal କିମ୍ବା Channel ର Frequency ପରିସର।

terms.definition: Message recovery using a frequency- and phase-aligned local carrier.

glosses.or: ମେଳ ଥିବା local Carrier ସହିତ Message ଫେରାଇବା।

terms.definition: An oscillator supplying a receiver reference signal.

glosses.or: Receiver ଭିତରେ Carrier reference ତିଆରି କରୁଥିବା source।

terms.definition: A scale factor used to correct recovered signal amplitude.

glosses.or: Recovery ପରେ Message amplitude ସୁଧାରିବାର ଗୁଣକ।

terms.definition: A filter that retains lower frequencies and attenuates higher frequencies.

glosses.or: କମ Frequency ରଖି ଉଚ୍ଚ Frequency କମାଉଥିବା Filter।

terms.definition: A specified frequency marking a filter response boundary; for this Butterworth filter, the minus-3-dB point.

glosses.or: Filter response ର ନିର୍ଦ୍ଦିଷ୍ଟ transition reference frequency।

terms.definition: An output phase shift behind its input at a particular frequency.

glosses.or: Input ସହିତ ତୁଳନାରେ Output phase ପଛରେ ରହିବା।

terms.definition: Relative phase mismatch between receiver and transmitter carriers.

glosses.or: ଦୁଇ Carrier ମଧ୍ୟରେ ଆବଶ୍ୟକ ମେଳଠାରୁ Phase ତଫାତ।

terms.definition: A difference between receiver and transmitter carrier frequencies.

glosses.or: Receiver ଓ Transmitter carrier frequency ଅଲଗା ହେବା।

terms.definition: A varying signal envelope caused by interaction of nearby frequencies.

glosses.or: Frequency ତଫାତ ଯୋଗୁଁ Signal amplitude ର ସମୟଭିତ୍ତିକ ପରିବର୍ତ୍ତନ।

terms.definition: Modulation in which instantaneous frequency deviation follows the message.

glosses.or: Message ଅନୁସାରେ instantaneous Carrier frequency ବଦଳାଇବା।

terms.definition: The maximum departure of instantaneous frequency from the carrier frequency.

glosses.or: Carrier frequency ଠାରୁ ସର୍ବାଧିକ Frequency ପରିବର୍ତ୍ତନ।

terms.definition: An approximate occupied-bandwidth estimate of 2*(frequency deviation + highest message frequency).

glosses.or: Angle modulation bandwidth ପାଇଁ ଏକ engineering approximation।

terms.definition: Modulation in which instantaneous phase deviation follows the message.

glosses.or: Message ଅନୁସାରେ instantaneous Carrier phase ବଦଳାଇବା।

terms.definition: The proportionality factor linking message amplitude to phase deviation.

glosses.or: Message ପ୍ରତି unit ପାଇଁ Phase ପରିବର୍ତ୍ତନର ଗୁଣକ।

terms.definition: Modulation represented through carrier frequency or phase changes.

glosses.or: Frequency କିମ୍ବା Phase ବଦଳାଇ ତଥ୍ୟ ପଠାଇବା।

practicals.title: DSB-SC Modulation & coherent demodulation
practicals.aim: Construct a DSB-SC transmitter and coherent receiver, compare signals, and diagnose a controlled carrier mismatch.
apparatus: Browser and MathWorks account with MATLAB/Simulink access
Saved model workspace; no physical hardware required

steps.checkpoint: Confirm the selected experiment and saved model reference before pointing.

steps.instruction: Place the Message and Carrier sources
steps.checkpoint: Message and Carrier Sine Wave blocks are present.

steps.instruction: Set source frequencies, amplitudes and phases
steps.checkpoint: Message: amplitude 1, 2*pi*100 rad/s, phase 0; Carrier: amplitude 1, 2*pi*2000 rad/s, phase pi/2; both bias 0.
Message and Carrier connect to distinct Product inputs; no DC carrier offset is added.

steps.instruction: Build the local carrier and receiver Product
steps.checkpoint: Local carrier matches amplitude 1, 2*pi*2000 rad/s and phase pi/2; modulated signal and local carrier enter receiver Product.

steps.instruction: Add the lowpass stage and Gain 2
steps.checkpoint: Transfer Fcn coefficients match the specified second-order 500 Hz Butterworth filter; following Gain is 2.

steps.instruction: Connect and label the observation scopes
steps.checkpoint: Scopes show sources, modulated output, and original versus recovered message on separate input ports.

steps.instruction: Set simulation duration and maximum step
steps.checkpoint: StopTime 0.1 s, variable-step ode45, MaxStep 1e-5 s.
The selected model completes a run without an error; evidence records the current parameter version.
After startup, recovered message is near 100 Hz and unit amplitude, with predicted filter phase lag and small residual ripple.
Student sets Local carrier Phase to pi, reruns, and observes suppression of the message component with possible high-frequency residual.
Local carrier Phase returns to pi/2; verified rerun restores recovery; model saved externally; student explains carrier alignment.

practicals.expected: Baseline recovery is approximately a unit-amplitude 100 Hz message after startup, with predicted filter phase lag and finite residual ripple. A relative 90-degree receiver phase fault suppresses the ideal message-band component; restoration recovers it.
practicals.predictionPrompt: Predict the original, DSB-SC and recovered waveforms before running; predict how a relative 90-degree receiver phase fault changes recovery.

faultCards.symptom: Transmitter looks correct, but recovered message nearly disappears after receiver phase change.
faultCards.cause: Local carrier phase pi versus baseline pi/2 creates 90-degree relative phase error.
faultCards.fix: Student restores local phase to pi/2, reruns and compares steady-state outputs.

faultCards.symptom: Recovered message varies over time despite a stable transmitter.
faultCards.cause: Local carrier frequency 2010 Hz differs from 2000 Hz transmitter carrier.
faultCards.fix: Student matches local carrier frequency to 2000 Hz, expressed as 2*pi*2000 rad/s.

faultCards.symptom: Recovered 100 Hz message is strongly attenuated.
faultCards.cause: Lowpass cutoff was reduced from 500 Hz to 50 Hz.
faultCards.fix: Student restores both numerator and denominator to the 500 Hz filter values.

vivaPrompts: Why keep the message bias at zero?
Why use a local carrier in the receiver?
Why is the baseline recovery gain two?
Why are the original and recovered traces shifted?
Why does a 90-degree relative phase error suppress recovery?
